name: Adam Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI firms, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in by half seven at Northfield High, a big state secondary with about 1,400 kids, and I teach history to Years 9 to 13. Five lessons on a heavy day, a duty on the yard at lunch, then marking or a meeting until five. I'm also the union rep for our building, so people come and find me when something's not right. The best bit is when a Year 10 actually argues with me about the causes of the First World War and has a point.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The paperwork, honestly. Data drops every six weeks, behaviour logs, emails from parents at ten at night. The teaching I'd do for free some days; the spreadsheets they'd have to pay me double for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the staffroom for two years: told you so. It was a fancy autocomplete and they sold it like the second coming. I'd probably post something sarky in the union group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I get to keep doing the job I trained for, which is a relief. I never wanted a machine marking my Year 11 essays. My pay stays on the scale, my partner Lena keeps nursing, and we carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep teaching the way I teach, paper and pen, and push back if the head tries to buy another AI marking package with money we need for teaching assistants. I'd keep putting a bit into savings each month like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest. I'd still be tired on a Thursday, but that's teaching, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the school buying AI marking packages. What's happened with that so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year the school trialled software that writes report comments. Our report-writing program called a boy who'd been excluded twice 'a joy to have in class'. We binned it after one term, and I was the one who said it in the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that still worries you, outside of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Class sizes, mostly. I've got 32 in my Year 9 group and the room fits 28. That's a money problem, not a robot problem, and it'll still be there in any of your pictures.

say: I'd tell the staffroom **I told you so** about the hype.
I'd say the school should spend on **teaching assistants**, not software.
think: I'm **relieved**, because I keep the job I actually trained for.
My pay and my partner's **nursing income** both look steady in this world.
do: Keep teaching with **paper and pen** and no AI tools.
Push back as **union rep** if leaders buy more AI software.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a bit of smugness about being right.
S0.quote: Our report-writing program called a boy who'd been excluded twice 'a joy to have in class'.
fieldNote: His identity rests on being the **sceptic** who was right about edtech.
The real pressure he names is **class size**, which is about budgets, not AI.
Secure pay, savings and a nurse partner make **calm** fit here.

steps.text: Keep teaching history with paper essays and no AI marking
Argue at union meetings against buying AI report software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loud: this is a funding cut wearing a lab coat. If software does the planning and marking, the next step is bigger classes with fewer of us. I'd raise it at the union branch meeting before the head raises it in the staff briefing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the kids still need a person in the room, so I'm not going anywhere. But my job changes into watching screens and checking what a machine wrote. I'd hate that, and I'd be bad at it, because I've never touched these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get the union to push for a written agreement on how AI is used, so it can't be used to judge us or cut posts. I'd keep teaching the same way. I'd probably go on one of the training days if they made it compulsory, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the trust took over the school and nobody knew what would change. My job's probably safe, but the ground's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the report comments program. What if that sort of thing gets good enough to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be told to use it, and I'd use it as little as I can. If a machine writes thirty reports in a minute, I'd still read every one, because a parent will notice if it's wrong. That's more work, not less, at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northfield would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin team. Our exams officer, Brenda, and the two ladies in the office do exactly the booking and checking that card talks about. And the cover supervisors, because a chatbot lesson plan makes them look cheap to replace.

say: I'd call it a **funding cut** dressed up as progress.
I'd tell colleagues to get a **written agreement** on AI before leaders act.
think: I think my **job is safe** because kids need an adult in the room.
I'd struggle, because I've **never used** these tools and don't want to.
do: Push the **union branch** for a written AI policy within the first term.
Attend **compulsory training** only, and check every AI-written report by hand.
feel: **Uneasy**, like waiting to hear what a new academy trust will change.
S1.quote: If software does the planning and marking, the next step is bigger classes with fewer of us.
fieldNote: He reads every change through **staffing and budgets**, as a union rep would.
He worries more for **office staff** than for himself, which fits his politics.
He admits he'd be **bad at** the new tools, a rare honest crack in the sceptic armour.

steps.text: Table a motion for a written AI agreement at the union branch
Keep planning his own history lessons without software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public control of this stuff, now, not after the fact. I'd be posting petitions and asking our MP where the plan is. You can't hand children's education to whatever company wins the race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? It scares me. If a machine can explain the Cold War better than me, and cheaper, the people counting money will notice inside a year. I'm 27 and I'd planned forty years of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw everything at the union campaign: demands for teacher-to-pupil ratios written into law. I'd stop spending on anything big, no new car, and keep our savings where they are. I'd also talk to the local Labour councillors, since schools funding runs through them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. It's like being told the building's on fire while you're halfway through a lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said thinking work goes first and robots three years later. How much of your day is thinking work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it, if I'm honest. Planning, marking, explaining, writing reports, that's all thinking. The hands-on part is keeping 32 teenagers safe and in their seats. So I'd get the 3 years before robots, maybe, as a sort of supervisor, and that's not a job I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we can still buy a place together. We've been saving for a deposit for three years. Lena would say nurses will be fine, robots or not, and she's probably right, so it would be my income that wobbles.

say: I'd demand **public control** of AI in schools straight away.
I'd ask our MP where the **government plan** is.
think: I think budget holders would **replace me** within a year if AI teaches cheaper.
I'd lose the **forty-year career** I planned at 27.
do: Campaign through the union for **legal class ratios** in the first months.
Freeze **big spending** like a new car and keep savings untouched.
feel: Frightened and **slightly sick**, like a fire alarm going off mid-lesson.
S2.quote: If a machine can explain the Cold War better than me, and cheaper, the people counting money will notice inside a year.
fieldNote: Two years gives him **no time**, and he has no AI skills to fall back on.
He sees the robot gap leaving him as a **supervisor**, which he'd find hollow.
Lena's steady nursing job is the household's **anchor**, and he says so.

steps.text: Lead a union campaign for class ratios written into law
Lobby local councillors and the MP on school funding
Put off buying a car and hold deposit savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, a bit calmer: we've got five years, so let's write the rules now. I'd want a law that a qualified teacher stands in every classroom. I'd say that at conference, not just online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still be teaching in 2031, but in a different shape. Maybe one teacher with three AI screens and sixty kids. That's not what I signed up for, and I'd be asking whether I want to be that person at 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year on the union side, getting an agreement locked in before it's needed. I'd start looking at jobs that are mostly people, like pastoral or safeguarding roles, where you deal with kids in crisis. And we'd still try to buy the flat, but a cheaper one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking. There's room to move, I just don't like where the room leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is double the warning of the last one. What does that extra time buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A union rule on paper, and time to get into pastoral work, which is hands-on with people. A head of year spends half the day sorting out fights and phoning social workers. Sorting out fights is harder to hand to a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI. Would that change with five years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a little, grudgingly. I'd let a colleague like Priya show me how it does seating plans. But I'd still refuse to let it mark essays, that's the line for me.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to write the rules.
I'd argue for a law putting **a qualified teacher** in every classroom.
think: I expect to still teach in 2031, but with **sixty kids** and screens.
I'd question whether I want to be **that teacher** at 32.
do: Secure a **union agreement** on AI staffing within the first year.
Apply for **pastoral roles** like head of year over the next two years.
feel: **Anxious** but in control, because there's still room to move.
S3.quote: A head of year spends half the day sorting out fights and phoning social workers. Sorting out fights is harder to hand to a screen.
fieldNote: Extra time turns his anger into **planning**, mostly through the union.
He'd move towards **pastoral work**, the people-heavy side of school.
He'll bend a little on **AI tools** but draws a line at essay marking.

steps.text: Negotiate a school-wide AI staffing agreement through the union
Apply for a head of year or safeguarding post
Buy a cheaper flat than planned with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for a decent government to plan for this. Retrain people, protect jobs, share the gains. If it goes badly, that's a choice someone made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when it lands, and I'd have most of my career still ahead. So it does worry me, maybe more than the fast one in a way, because I'd have to decide what to do with my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep up the union work, because that's where I'm useful. I'd save hard, maybe pay off a chunk of a mortgage early. Around year five I'd look seriously at social work training, because it's people, it's hands-on, and robots come last there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady, low worry. Ten years is like knowing your boiler's old and will go sometime. You don't panic, but you check the savings every winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, would you think about leaving teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it, yes. I wouldn't jump, I'm not that kind of person. But I'd want something lined up by my mid-thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Northfield to do with those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train us properly, and keep the staff together. Use the time to make classes smaller, not to cut teachers. If the school treats the decade as a countdown to redundancies, I'll fight it.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for **government planning** and retraining.
I'd call a bad outcome **a choice** someone made.
think: At 37 I'd still have **most of my career** left to fill.
A slow arrival means I'd have to **decide my future** myself.
do: Keep teaching and **union work** for the first several years.
Overpay the **mortgage** to cut debt early.
Look into **social work training** around year five.
feel: A **steady, low worry**, like an old boiler that will fail someday.
S4.quote: Ten years is like knowing your boiler's old and will go sometime. You don't panic, but you check the savings every winter.
fieldNote: The long runway still leaves a **mid-career gap** he'll have to fill.
His plan B is **social work**, chosen because it is people-heavy.
He wants the decade used for **smaller classes**, not redundancies.

steps.text: Keep teaching history and running the union branch
Overpay the mortgage each year to cut the debt

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years is nothing when you've got no AI skills and a deposit you're saving for. What would help is a legal rule that every class has a qualified teacher, and a union strong enough to make it stick.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. Everyone talks about our jobs, but a fourteen-year-old who's taught by a chatbot all day isn't learning how to sit with other people. Teachers are the only adults some of my students talk to properly all week.

headlineQuote: Teachers are the only adults some of my students talk to properly all week.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old **history teacher** and union rep at a large city secondary.
He has **never used AI** tools and is proud of teaching with paper and pen.
He feels **calm** if AI stalls, and uneasy as it takes over planning and marking.
Fast AGI **alarms** him, because nearly all his work is thinking work.
With more time he'd lean on **the union** and move towards pastoral or social work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to build new skills.
whatWouldHelp: A **legal rule** that every class has a qualified teacher.
A **strong union** that makes that rule stick.
